name: Pulvinar
summary: The large posterior cushion of the thalamus overhanging the midbrain and the geniculate bodies. It is the association nucleus for vision and attention, reciprocally connected with the parietal, temporal and occipital association cortices and the superior colliculus. Left pulvinar lesions contribute to thalamic aphasia and right ones to neglect; bilateral pulvinar hyperintensity on diffusion imaging is the signature of variant Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease, and it is the thalamic target of Fabry disease and some metabolic disorders.

anatomy.location: Posterior pole of the thalamus above the superior colliculus and behind the ventral posterior nuclei, medial to the lateral geniculate body and bordering the atrium of the lateral ventricle.

efferents.to: parietal, temporal and occipital association cortex

function: Visual attention and salience, integration of visual and other sensory information with the parietal and temporal cortices, contributions to language (left) and spatial attention (right).

imaging.normalAppearance: The rounded posterior end of the thalamus on axial slices at the level of the atria; symmetric brightness on DWI/FLAIR is abnormal.

pathology.finding: Bilateral symmetric pulvinar hyperintensity on DWI/FLAIR, greater than the anterior putamen, with the hockey-stick sign when the dorsomedial nuclei join.
Pulvinar and lateral geniculate restriction with a field defect and sensory disturbance.
T1-bright pulvinar (calcification) in a young patient with strokes.

imaging.sequenceOfChoice: DWI and FLAIR; CT for calcification

lesionEffects.mechanism: Association connections with the parietal and temporal cortex

lesionEffects.deficit: Rapidly progressive dementia with pulvinar sign

examination: Language: fluent output with paraphasias and preserved repetition in thalamic aphasia
pearls: Thalamic aphasia is fluent with preserved repetition, unlike Broca or Wernicke aphasia
Bilateral bright pulvinars in a young person with psychiatric symptoms and ataxia: variant CJD
